content.text: what's save_lobu_app_state restore_lobu_app_result and render_lobu_view, do we actually need them

I’ll trace those three tools from their definitions through callers, runtime behavior, and client-visible metadata. I’m using the Lobu operator skill because this is a monorepo/API-surface audit, and I’ll keep it read-only.

The prior release context says these were intentionally split into two layers: `render_lobu_view` is model-facing, while the save/restore helpers are hidden app plumbing. I’m verifying whether current source and actual call paths still justify each helper, rather than assuming that earlier design is still necessary.

Current `origin/main` confirms the split, but it also shows the cost: the restore/save pair exists mainly to survive ChatGPT iframe reloads and missing/reused host tool-call identity. It adds an encrypted snapshot table, retention cleanup, capability binding, and a large client-side reconciliation state machine. I’m checking whether the current MCP Apps/OpenAI host contracts now offer a simpler native replacement.

Short version: keep `render_lobu_view`; plan to remove the other two.

| Tool | Purpose | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| `render_lobu_view` | Model-facing tool that turns selected data or an approval into a sanitized rich card with a text fallback. | Keep |
| `restore_lobu_app_result` | App-only workaround that reloads an encrypted, 30-day snapshot when ChatGPT loses a historical card’s result. It never reruns the operation. | Probably remove |
| `save_lobu_app_state` | App-only helper that binds snapshots to host card IDs and persists pagination/disclosure state. | Remove with restore |

Why:

- `render_lobu_view` is the correct boundary. Ordinary SQL/SDK/data calls stay headless; the model explicitly renders only a useful final result. OpenAI’s current guidance recommends exactly this decoupled data-tool/render-tool pattern. [OpenAI UI guide](https://developers.openai.com/plugins/build/chatgpt-ui#separate-data-processing-from-ui-rendering)
- The save/restore pair was built around older ChatGPT reload problems: empty replayed results, missing tool information, and reused card IDs. It created the snapshot table and a substantial reconciliation state machine in [mcp-app-result-snapshots.ts](/Users/burakemre/Code/lobu/packages/server/src/mcp-app-result-snapshots.ts:169) and [host.tsx](/Users/burakemre/Code/lobu/packages/owletto/src/mcp-apps/_shared/host.tsx:381).
- It is not meaningfully portable: server snapshot identity depends on OpenAI’s private `openai/session` metadata. Other MCP hosts do not get this fallback.
- ChatGPT now provides `toolOutput`, `toolResponseMetadata`, `widgetState`, and `setWidgetState`; Lobu already caches the displayed result there. Current OpenAI guidance explicitly says pagination, expanded panels, and sort order are ephemeral UI state and should remain in the UI. [State guidance](https://developers.openai.com/plugins/build/chatgpt-ui#manage-state)
- Persisting that state server-side duplicates potentially sensitive rendered data for 30 days and adds database, cleanup, capability-binding, collision, and concurrency machinery.

The helpers appear in raw `tools/list` because the iframe must call them, but `visibility: ["app"]` means compliant hosts hide them from the model. [MCP Apps specification](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/ext-apps/blob/main/specification/2026-01-26/apps.mdx)

My recommendation: retain `render_lobu_view`; replace save/restore with local React state plus ChatGPT `widgetState`, accepting reset-on-reload for other hosts. Before deletion, run a focused compatibility matrix covering hard reload, reopening an old conversation, reused iframe, multiple identical cards, and approval-result replacement. Removing them also changes the MCP surface and drops a table, so it needs an explicit approved proposal first.

I checked current `origin/main` and production revision `da239ccc…`; the pair is wired and active, not dead code—just likely obsolete compatibility infrastructure.

Yes—if the MCP card has Approve/Reject buttons, we still need `resolve_approval`.

They represent different authority boundaries:

```text
Agent → request_approval(proposal)
          ↓ durable pending approval
Human → resolve_approval(approve | reject)
          ↓ capability checked
       operation resumes
```

- `request_approval` is model-visible. It creates a durable pending approval and returns its card.
- `resolve_approval` is app-only. The model must never be able to approve its own request. It requires the hidden, user/session/event-bound capability, as the current implementation does in [mcp_app.ts](/Users/burakemre/Code/lobu/packages/server/src/tools/mcp_app.ts:602).
- `get_approval` is optional for reopening an existing approval or refreshing its status.

We could eliminate `resolve_approval` only if the card has no inline buttons and merely links to Lobu, where the normal web UI performs the decision.

One important distinction: when `run_sdk` already produces a pending approval, calling `request_approval` must not create another one. In that path the appropriate operation is `get_approval(run_id)`. Therefore the clean complete surface is probably:

- `request_approval`: create a new standalone proposal requiring human judgment.
- `get_approval`: display an already-existing approval.
- `resolve_approval`: capability-protected, app-only human decision.
- `save_memory`: durable accepted knowledge/artifacts.
- No `render_lobu_view`.

I would keep request and resolve separate rather than using one `action=request|resolve` tool, because their callers and authority are fundamentally different.

content.text:
Yes—ChatGPT can continue after the user clicks the approval button. The user does not need to manually type.

The widget can:

1. Call the app-only `resolve_approval` tool to record the authoritative decision.
2. After success, send a follow-up conversation message:

```ts
await callTool("resolve_approval", {
  run_id,
  decision: "approve",
});

await sendFollowUpMessage({
  prompt: `I approved Lobu run ${run_id}. Continue the task and report the result.`,
});
```

These are both supported by the portable MCP Apps bridge: `tools/call` performs the action and `ui/message` sends the follow-up. ChatGPT exposes compatibility aliases as `window.openai.callTool` and `window.openai.sendFollowUpMessage`. [Official OpenAI documentation](https://developers.openai.com/plugins/build/chatgpt-ui#prefer-shared-fields-and-methods)

The important boundary is:

- `ui/message` continues the conversation, but it should not constitute the approval.
- `resolve_approval` records the exact, permission-checked decision.
- The follow-up creates a new ChatGPT turn; it does not resurrect the original model execution. Lobu’s underlying run can resume independently after approval.

So we don’t necessarily need a tool specifically named `resolve_approval`, but we do need an authenticated app-only mutation somewhere. The current thin tool is a good implementation because it validates the hidden capability before calling Lobu’s canonical approval handler.

We could remove it only if:

- The card links to Lobu and approval happens there, or
- The user types “approve run 123,” and ChatGPT invokes another model-visible approval tool.

The second option is slower, less deterministic, and exposes approval functionality to the model. My recommendation is therefore:

```text
request_approval → durable card
user clicks Approve
resolve_approval → authoritative mutation
ui/message → “Approved; continue”
ChatGPT continues automatically
```

That gives us one-click approval without trusting conversation text as the approval record.

just to understand. is the approval only way to do bidirectional? can't the mcp clients send custom form etc to the user

I’m checking the current MCP Apps/ChatGPT contract because the distinction is subtle: app widgets can absolutely collect arbitrary structured input, but “continue the model turn afterward” is a separate host capability. I’m using the ChatGPT Apps and OpenAI docs guidance to separate those two layers accurately.

The key distinction is now clear: MCP has both a blocking structured-input mechanism and a rich custom-UI mechanism, but today they are not the same primitive. I’m checking whether ChatGPT publicly documents support for core MCP elicitation before saying Lobu could rely on it.

No—approval is only one product-specific use of bidirectional MCP UI.

There are three related mechanisms:

1. Custom MCP App forms

An MCP server can provide arbitrary HTML UI: forms, dropdowns, tables, editors, multi-step wizards, charts, etc. The client renders it in a sandboxed iframe. When the user submits, the app calls an MCP tool through `tools/call`. That tool could be `save_memory`, `update_settings`, `create_report`, or `resolve_approval`. [MCP Apps explicitly supports interactive forms and bidirectional communication.](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/extensions/apps/overview)

2. Continue the conversation

After submitting, the app can send `ui/message`—`sendFollowUpMessage` in ChatGPT—which posts a user-authored message and triggers the model to continue. It can also use `ui/update-model-context` to update future context without immediately starting a turn. [OpenAI documents these as standard MCP Apps capabilities.](https://developers.openai.com/plugins/build/chatgpt-ui#prefer-shared-fields-and-methods)

3. Core MCP elicitation

MCP also has `elicitation/create`: the server supplies a restricted JSON Schema and the client generates a native form. This can block the original request until the user answers, but it supports only relatively flat structured input—not arbitrary custom HTML. [MCP elicitation specification.](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/draft/client/elicitation)

The current gap is that a fully custom MCP App form does not protocol-guarantee that the original agent turn pauses until submission. The usual reliable pattern is:

```text
tool returns custom form
        ↓
user completes form
        ↓
app calls app-only MCP tool
        ↓
server persists result
        ↓
app sends ui/message
        ↓
model continues
```

That is exactly what Lobu approval now does. `resolve_approval` is not “the bidirectional mechanism”; it is simply the domain-specific mutation endpoint behind that particular form.

For Lobu, I’d use:

- `save_memory` → may render a memory-specific editor, enrichment form, or saved-memory confirmation.
- `get_approval` → renders the durable approval.
- `resolve_approval` → records the approval decision.
- Future rich workflows → their own semantic tools, such as `configure_digest` or `update_memory`, instead of routing everything through `save_memory`.

So yes, `save_memory` can itself be interactive and bidirectional. It just shouldn’t become the universal form/action tool, because the tool name should describe the actual durable operation, authorization boundary, and audit event.

Also, only MCP Apps-capable clients can render custom HTML. Plain MCP clients can use ordinary tools and possibly schema-generated elicitation forms, so Lobu should continue capability-detecting and providing a headless fallback.

They can share the same widget and interaction machinery; the real question is whether they should share one model-visible tool contract. I’m checking that boundary against the current Apps guidance and Lobu’s existing tool semantics before giving you a firm recommendation.

Yes—merged at the UI layer, but not ideally as one tool.

They already share the same Lobu widget contract and renderer. The distinction is backend semantics:

- `save_memory` creates a new append-only memory event. It requires `mcp:write`.
- `get_approval` reads an existing pending run. It requires only `mcp:read`.
- `resolve_approval` performs the protected human decision and remains app-only.

Overloading `save_memory` with something like:

```ts
{ operation: "save", content: ... }
{ operation: "get_approval", run_id: ... }
```

would mix read/write permissions, annotations, schemas, audit semantics, and model intent. Asking to view an approval would misleadingly invoke “save memory.” OpenAI’s current guidance similarly recommends defining the tool contract around narrow user outcomes before designing the widget. [Official ChatGPT Apps guidance](https://learn.chatgpt.com/use-cases/chatgpt-apps#common-pitfalls)

The coherent alternatives are:

1. Current design — recommended:

```text
save_memory       create durable memory
get_approval      open durable approval
resolve_approval  app-only decision
```

2. A truly memory-centric design:

```text
save_memory
open_memory_item
```

Here approvals, saved notes, reports, and other durable events are all memory items, and `open_memory_item({ id })` selects the appropriate card. But that starts resembling `render_lobu_view` again—just with a clearer, memory-scoped contract.

So your instinct was right about consolidation: there should be one shared Lobu card system. But `save_memory` should not also pretend to be a read operation. If we later canonicalize approvals as addressable memory items, replacing `get_approval` with `open_memory_item` would be the clean merge.

| Lobu interaction stage | External ChatGPT coverage |
|---|---|
| Agent creates durable notification/question | Yes, through Lobu’s backend |
| Push notification to an idle user | Not through documented MCP Apps APIs |
| Render `json_template` | Yes, through Lobu’s MCP App widget |
| Custom buttons/forms | Yes, through app-only `tools/call` |
| Resume the original Lobu agent | Yes, if the called Lobu tool persists the answer and resumes its run |
| Continue the ChatGPT conversation | Yes, through `ui/message` |
| Inbox/history/reopen later | Lobu remains canonical unless we expose discovery tools |

MCP Apps renders a widget when a UI-enabled tool is called; it supports forms, custom interfaces, button-triggered tools, and live updates while mounted. [MCP Apps overview](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/extensions/apps/overview) OpenAI’s documented component APIs cover calling tools and sending follow-up messages, but do not document a server-originated mechanism for injecting a new card into a dormant ChatGPT conversation. That last point is an inference from the current public API surface, so we should not promise ChatGPT push delivery. The architecture should therefore be:

```text
Lobu agent
   │ notifications.send / save_memory
   ▼
durable Lobu event + pending run
   ├── Lobu inbox / Slack / native notification
   └── ChatGPT discovers or opens it
               │
               ▼
       shared MCP App renderer
               │ button/form
               ▼
       app-only response tool
          ├── resumes original Lobu run
          └── ui/message continues ChatGPT
```

This broader use case changes the naming recommendation slightly: `get_approval` is only one subtype. The more reusable external-client contract would be:

- `save_memory` / `notifications.send`: create durable content or interactions.
- `get_interaction`: list/open a durable notification, question, approval, or custom template.
- `respond_to_interaction`: app-only, signed action that resumes the underlying Lobu run.

Approval becomes an interaction type rather than its own presentation system.

One safety boundary matters: `json_template` buttons should carry declarative action IDs, not arbitrary MCP tool names and arguments. Lobu should resolve those IDs server-side against allowed, server-authored actions. That preserves the human approval and authorization boundary.

So: ChatGPT can be an excellent interaction surface, but Lobu remains the durable notification/router/inbox. If external clients need full parity, generalizing `get_approval` into `get_interaction` is cleaner than merging it into `save_memory`.

tell me if elicitation would make the experience better? how does eliciations work in claude code

Yes—elicitation would make the experience noticeably better in Claude Code, but specifically for **immediate interaction during an active tool call**. It would not replace Lobu’s durable approval system.

In Claude Code, the flow is:

1. Claude calls a Lobu MCP tool.
2. While processing it, Lobu sends `elicitation/create` with a message and a flat JSON schema.
3. Claude Code pauses the tool call and opens a native dialog.
4. The user submits, declines, or cancels.
5. Claude Code returns that structured response to Lobu.
6. The original tool continues and returns its result.
7. Claude automatically continues the same conversational turn.

For example:

```text
Claude calls: deploy_release

Lobu needs confirmation:
┌─────────────────────────────────┐
│ Approve production deployment?  │
│ Environment: Production         │
│ Release: v2.4.0                 │
│                                 │
│       Cancel   Reject   Approve │
└─────────────────────────────────┘

User clicks Approve
→ deploy_release continues
→ result returns to Claude
→ Claude explains what happened
```

Claude Code supports both:

- Form mode: text fields, booleans, enums, simple selections.
- URL mode: Claude asks permission to open a browser URL for authentication or sensitive input.

Support was added in Claude Code 2.1.76, including `Elicitation` and `ElicitationResult` hooks for controlling responses. ([Claude Code changelog](https://github.com/anthropics/claude-code/blob/main/CHANGELOG.md))

Where it improves Lobu:

- Asking for one missing value without failing the tool and starting another turn.
- Selecting an organization, connection, account, deployment target, or option.
- Immediate confirmation while an operation is running.
- Automatically continuing Claude after the answer.
- Native Claude UI without maintaining an MCP App widget.

Where it does not help:

- The approver might respond hours later.
- Another team member must approve.
- The request must reach Slack, mobile, Lobu inbox, or another client.
- We need durable audit history and retries.
- We need custom presentation, nested forms, `jsonTemplate`, previews, or rich buttons.
- ChatGPT does not advertise verified elicitation support.

The best Lobu architecture would therefore be:

```text
Durable Lobu interaction
        │
        ├── Claude Code/Codex/VS Code → native elicitation
        ├── ChatGPT/Claude Desktop    → MCP App approval card
        └── unsupported client        → text + Open in Lobu link
```

Lobu would remain the source of truth. Elicitation would only be a client adapter: persist the approval first, elicit immediately if supported, resolve the persisted approval from the response, then continue the original tool call.

So my verdict is: **worth adding eventually as progressive enhancement**, particularly for Claude Code. It would make synchronous approvals feel much smoother and could avoid an explicit `resolve_approval` model call there. But it should sit on top of the current durable approval machinery—not replace it—because elicitation is active-session, single-client, and short-lived. The client capability must also be checked before using it. ([MCP elicitation specification](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/draft/client/elicitation))

content.text: I’m continuing from the live failure boundary: the form itself renders, but ChatGPT’s outer loading overlay never releases. The legacy Skybridge and external-script experiments are ruled out; I’m reverting that temporary scaffolding and fixing the standard MCP Apps handshake in the bootstrap so ChatGPT sees the app as initialized before the compressed UI finishes loading.

The transport is plain JSON-RPC over `postMessage`, so the fix can stay standards-based. I’ve confirmed we do not need a ChatGPT-only resource or elicitation: the packed loader can complete `ui/initialize`, retain the initial tool result, and proxy `tools/call`, `ui/message`, `ui/open-link`, and size updates while the React bundle unpacks. I’m also replacing the approval card’s portaled enum menu with a native select inside MCP cards, which removes the iframe-clipping failure rather than trying to outguess host dimensions.

content.text: The fresh-call trace confirms this is not Lobu’s React state or the form: ChatGPT invokes its legacy `setWidgetData` before a result exists, then drops the standard `tool-result` notification if the sandbox adapter has not initialized. This is adapter packaging, not a second product/tool contract.

content.text: I found the exact reason the setting ignored automation: current Chrome deliberately rejects that secure toggle unless the click is marked as a hardware-input event with no sender process. I’m using that narrow input path only for this one toggle; this avoids restarting Chrome, copying profiles, or touching cookies.

The logs now show the real cause: `server-integration-bun` repeatedly times out trying to `TRUNCATE` the shared test database while another test still holds locks. So yes, Kubernetes would be better—but specifically with isolation:

- One ephemeral namespace and Postgres instance/database per PR preview.

- TTL cleanup for preview namespaces and explicit concurrency cancellation only for the same PR.

content.text: I found the concrete production-only bug: Lobu’s canonical MCP URL is `https://lobu.ai/mcp`, but the v35 resource derives its JS/CSS base from that request host. `https://lobu.ai/mcp-apps/...` returns 404; the assets actually live at `https://app.lobu.ai/mcp-apps/...`. That explains why local/tailscale passed and the production ChatGPT iframe stayed blank. I’m opening a narrow follow-up fix with a regression test for the canonical proxy URL, then I’ll rerun review/CI, merge, roll out, and repeat this same ChatGPT approval.

I found the real permission boundary. ChatGPT’s OAuth grant is correctly only `mcp:read mcp:write`, while `notifications.send` is currently classified as `mcp:admin`; the server then masks that scope error as generic `-32603`. So the v36 UI fix itself hasn’t failed—ChatGPT cannot create the test approval under its granted scope.

The safe product model is: keep ChatGPT non-admin, let an external agent/workspace automation create the approval, and let ChatGPT review/resolve it. I’m using that path for this E2E now; I won’t silently broaden ChatGPT to org-admin access.
